description: Diet, sleep, alcohol, smoking and the long-term health risks of a sedentary lifestyle.
content_html:
Lifestyle and Its Impact on Health

The choices a person makes every day — what they eat, how much they move, how they sleep, whether they use recreational drugs — accumulate over time to shape their long-term health. These are known as lifestyle choices. Understanding which choices promote health and which ones damage it is fundamental to physical education because it connects the theory of the body to the reality of how people live. The spec identifies four key lifestyle factors: diet, activity level, work/rest/sleep balance, and the use of recreational drugs (alcohol and nicotine).

Diet

A balanced diet provides the energy and nutrients the body needs to function well. The key macronutrient proportions for a healthy, active individual are approximately 55–60% carbohydrates, 25–30% fats and 15–20% protein. Carbohydrates are the primary fuel for physical activity, particularly moderate-to-high-intensity exercise. Protein is essential for muscle repair and growth after training. Fats support hormone production, cell function and provide fuel for low-intensity, prolonged exercise. Vitamins and minerals (micronutrients) are needed in smaller amounts but support vital functions such as immune defence, oxygen transport (iron) and bone formation (calcium and vitamin D).

Poor diet choices can have serious long-term consequences. A diet consistently high in saturated fat and refined sugar raises low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, contributing to atherosclerosis and coronary heart disease. A high-calorie, low-nutrient diet causes weight gain and, if sustained, leads to obesity. A diet lacking in calcium and vitamin D weakens bones, increasing the risk of osteoporosis. Insufficient iron intake can cause anaemia, reducing the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood and impairing exercise performance.

Work/Rest/Sleep Balance

The body does not adapt to training during exercise — it adapts during rest and recovery. Insufficient sleep disrupts the release of growth hormone, which is essential for muscle repair. Chronically poor sleep is associated with weight gain (due to disrupted appetite hormones), increased injury risk and reduced concentration, which impairs the decision-making needed in sport. For athletes, 8–9 hours of sleep per night is generally recommended, though individual needs vary. An imbalanced lifestyle where work or social pressures chronically reduce sleep time can negate the benefits of regular training.

Key Fact

The four lifestyle factors are: diet (balanced nutrition vs poor food choices), activity level (regular exercise vs sedentary behaviour), work/rest/sleep balance (adequate recovery vs chronic sleep deprivation), and use of recreational drugs (abstaining vs smoking or alcohol use). Each factor can either protect health or increase risk of disease.

Recreational Drugs: Alcohol and Nicotine

Nicotine is the addictive substance in tobacco. Smoking damages the respiratory system progressively. The tar in cigarette smoke coats the alveoli, reducing the surface area available for gas exchange and lowering the efficiency of oxygen delivery to muscles. Carbon monoxide in smoke binds to haemoglobin in place of oxygen, further reducing the blood’s oxygen-carrying capacity. Long-term consequences of smoking include bronchitis (inflammation of the bronchi, causing persistent cough and breathlessness), emphysema (destruction of alveoli, causing severe breathlessness) and lung cancer. Smokers have significantly reduced cardiovascular endurance and are less able to sustain aerobic activity. A 16-year-old who smokes regularly will have measurably worse performance on a Cooper 12-minute run test than a non-smoking peer of the same training background.

Alcohol is a depressant drug that slows the central nervous system. Short-term effects relevant to sport include impaired reaction time, reduced coordination and decreased balance — all of which reduce performance and increase injury risk. Long-term excessive alcohol consumption damages the liver (cirrhosis), raises blood pressure, contributes to weight gain (alcohol is high in calories with no nutritional value) and weakens the immune system. Alcohol also disrupts sleep quality, compounding the recovery problems described above. Athletes who regularly consume alcohol in large quantities find that their cardiovascular fitness, strength adaptations and recovery rates all deteriorate over time.

Carbon monoxide from cigarette smoke binds to haemoglobin with an affinity 200 times greater than oxygen. This means a smoker’s haemoglobin is partially ‘blocked’ and cannot carry as much oxygen to working muscles. The result is that cardiac output must increase to compensate, raising heart rate for the same submaximal workload. The smoker’s maximum aerobic capacity (VO2 max) is measurably lower. Additionally, nicotine causes vasoconstriction — narrowing of blood vessels — which raises blood pressure and reduces blood flow to the working muscles. On a mark scheme, naming the mechanism (carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin; tar coats alveoli) earns more marks than simply stating “smoking reduces fitness.”

Sedentary Lifestyle and Its Consequences

A sedentary lifestyle is one that involves little or no regular physical activity. As a result of reduced energy expenditure, the body stores excess energy as fat, leading to being overweight or, in more serious cases, clinically obese. The consequences extend far beyond body weight. Without regular exercise, the cardiovascular system deteriorates: resting heart rate rises, blood pressure increases and the risk of coronary heart disease escalates significantly.

Sedentary individuals have lower insulin sensitivity, increasing the risk of type 2 diabetes. Inactivity weakens muscles through atrophy and reduces bone density, elevating the risk of osteoporosis. Posture deteriorates as postural muscles weaken from disuse, contributing to chronic back pain. Mental health is also affected: sedentary people have higher rates of depression and anxiety, partly because they miss the endorphin benefits of exercise and partly because sedentary activities (such as excessive screen time) displace social interaction and purposeful activity.

Students sometimes use these three terms interchangeably, but they have distinct meanings. Overweight refers to body mass above what is considered healthy for a person’s height (typically BMI > 25). Overfat refers specifically to excess body fat regardless of total weight — a heavily muscled athlete might be overweight by BMI but not overfat. Obese is a clinical classification (BMI > 30) associated with serious long-term health risks. The spec uses all three terms and a mark scheme will reward the correct term for the context described.

Key Fact

Consequences of a sedentary lifestyle include: overweight/obesity, coronary heart disease, high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes, osteoporosis, loss of muscle tone and poor posture, and depression/anxiety. These span all three dimensions of health and are all reducible through regular physical activity.
exam_tip_html: For questions about smoking and health, always name the specific mechanism rather than saying “it reduces fitness.” For example: “Carbon monoxide from tobacco smoke binds to haemoglobin, reducing the blood’s oxygen-carrying capacity.” That earns the mark — vague statements do not. For sedentary lifestyle questions, list consequences across different body systems (cardiovascular, skeletal, muscular, psychological) to demonstrate breadth. A common mistake is to list only physical consequences such as obesity; mark schemes also reward depression and anxiety as effects of inactivity. When using the terms overweight, overfat and obese, use them precisely — they are not synonyms.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The four key lifestyle factors are diet, activity level, work/rest/sleep balance and use of recreational drugs. Positive choices in each area protect health; negative choices increase risk of long-term disease.
  • Smoking reduces oxygen delivery to muscles via carbon monoxide binding to haemoglobin and tar coating the alveoli; long-term consequences include bronchitis, emphysema and lung cancer. Alcohol impairs reaction time, coordination and sleep quality.
  • A sedentary lifestyle leads to obesity, coronary heart disease, high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes, osteoporosis, muscle loss and depression — consequences spanning all three dimensions of health.

practice_questions.text: State one long-term consequence of a sedentary lifestyle on cardiovascular health.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any valid cardiovascular consequence: increased risk of coronary heart disease / raised blood pressure / increased resting heart rate / increased risk of type 2 diabetes (credit as cardiovascular consequence via insulin resistance link).

1 mark for identifying lack of physical activity as the key feature (e.g. little or no regular exercise / predominantly inactive behaviour); 1 mark for contextualising with an example or the health consequence (e.g. typically involves prolonged sitting, screen time or desk-based work, leading to low energy expenditure and accumulation of excess body fat).

practice_questions.text: Describe how smoking reduces a performer's ability to sustain aerobic exercise.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for identifying that carbon monoxide in smoke binds to haemoglobin, reducing the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity; 1 mark for explaining that tar coats the alveoli, reducing the surface area for gas exchange and lowering the efficiency of oxygen absorption; 1 mark for stating the consequence for performance (the working muscles receive less oxygen, so the performer fatigues more quickly during sustained aerobic activity such as distance running).

practice_questions.text: Table 1 shows the average weekly hours of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity for two groups of 16-year-old students. Group A: 5.8 hours. Group B: 0.9 hours. Interpret what this data suggests about the likely long-term health outcomes for students in Group B.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly reading the data (Group B averages only 0.9 hours, far below Group A's 5.8 hours and below recommended guidelines); 1 mark for identifying at least one physical health consequence for Group B (e.g. increased risk of obesity / coronary heart disease / type 2 diabetes / osteoporosis); 1 mark for identifying a mental health consequence (e.g. increased risk of depression or anxiety due to lack of endorphin release); 1 mark for a comparative or evaluative statement (e.g. Group B students are at significantly greater long-term health risk than Group A students across multiple health dimensions).

practice_questions.text: A secondary school introduces a daily 20-minute active break for all students in response to concerns about sedentary behaviour. Assess whether this intervention is likely to improve students' health and wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Factors supporting and questioning the intervention are weighed; health benefits explained with mechanisms (e.g. daily moderate activity raises heart rate, improves cardiovascular fitness, reduces obesity risk, triggers endorphin release improving mood); limitations acknowledged (e.g. 20 minutes may be insufficient; intensity matters; benefits depend on whether students are sedentary outside school); reasoned judgement reached.

Secure: Benefits and limitations both present; mostly accurate physiological explanation; reasoned conclusion.

Developing: Mainly benefits described; limited physiological mechanism; little evaluation of whether the intervention is sufficient.

Emerging: Basic statement that exercise is good with little development.

Acceptable content in support: daily activity raises heart rate and improves cardiovascular fitness over time; endorphin release improves emotional wellbeing; structured movement reduces prolonged sitting; social interaction during the break improves social health. Limitations: 20 minutes is relatively short; benefit depends on intensity; students may still be sedentary for the other 23+ hours; the intervention does not address diet or sleep.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the extent to which lifestyle choices are the most important factor in determining a person's long-term health outcomes.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced evaluation across multiple lifestyle factors (diet, activity, sleep, alcohol/smoking); consideration of other determinants of health (genetics, socio-economic status, healthcare access); consistent sporting or health examples; justified conclusion that acknowledges lifestyle as highly important while recognising it is not the sole determinant.

Secure: At least three lifestyle factors covered; some acknowledgement of other health determinants; sporting examples present; conclusion reached.

Developing: Mainly lifestyle factors described with limited evaluation; other health determinants absent or minimal; argument largely one-sided.

Emerging: Basic list of lifestyle factors with no evaluative structure.

Agreeing (lifestyle is most important): diet, activity level, sleep and avoidance of alcohol/smoking account for the largest share of preventable disease; regular exercise reduces risk of CHD, obesity, type 2 diabetes, osteoporosis; smoking causes bronchitis/lung cancer; diet drives body composition.

Partial challenge: genetics influence susceptibility to disease regardless of lifestyle (e.g. familial hypercholesterolaemia); socio-economic factors limit access to healthy food and safe exercise spaces; access to healthcare affects early detection and treatment of disease. Conclusion: lifestyle choices are the single most modifiable and impactful factor for most people, but they interact with non-modifiable factors such as genetics and structural inequalities.

knowledge_checks.q: Which substance in cigarette smoke binds to haemoglobin and reduces oxygen delivery to muscles?
Which of the following is a long-term consequence of a sedentary lifestyle on the skeletal system?
Tar from cigarette smoke coats the _____, reducing the surface area available for gas exchange.
A diet high in saturated fat raises LDL cholesterol, increasing the risk of _____ disease.
Match each lifestyle factor to its associated health risk:
right: Impaired reaction time and liver damage

flashcard_questions.q: Name the four lifestyle factors identified in the spec.
flashcard_questions.a: Diet, activity level, work/rest/sleep balance, and recreational drug use.

flashcard_questions.q: How does carbon monoxide in cigarette smoke reduce exercise performance?
flashcard_questions.a: It binds to haemoglobin, reducing oxygen carried to working muscles.

flashcard_questions.q: What does tar in cigarette smoke do to the respiratory system?
flashcard_questions.a: It coats the alveoli, reducing the surface area for gas exchange.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two long-term health conditions caused by regular smoking.
How does alcohol affect reaction time in sport?
flashcard_questions.a: It slows the central nervous system, impairing reaction time and decision-making.
Little or no regular physical activity, typically involving prolonged sitting.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one cardiovascular consequence of a sedentary lifestyle.
flashcard_questions.a: Increased risk of coronary heart disease due to reduced cardiovascular fitness.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between overweight and obese?
flashcard_questions.a: Overweight is BMI above healthy range; obese is a clinical classification (BMI over 30).

flashcard_questions.q: How does insufficient sleep affect athletic performance?
flashcard_questions.a: It disrupts muscle repair via reduced growth hormone and impairs decision-making.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does poor diet increase the risk of anaemia in athletes?
flashcard_questions.a: Insufficient iron reduces haemoglobin production, lowering oxygen transport.

flashcard_questions.q: What macronutrient proportion is recommended for carbohydrates in a balanced diet?
flashcard_questions.a: 55 to 60 per cent of total energy intake.

flashcard_questions.q: How does a sedentary lifestyle affect mental health?
flashcard_questions.a: It increases risk of depression and anxiety by removing endorphin benefits of exercise.

glossary_terms.definition: Personal decisions that influence health and wellbeing, including diet, activity level, work/rest balance and use of recreational drugs.
A diet that contains the correct proportions of all essential nutrients to maintain health, support growth and provide energy.
A recreational drug found in tobacco smoke that is highly addictive and causes blood vessel constriction, raising blood pressure and heart rate.
A way of living that involves little or no regular physical activity, typically involving prolonged sitting or very low-energy pursuits.
Having a body mass index (BMI) above the healthy range due to excess body fat.
